findings.paper_title: General Fund Finance Update - 2026/27 Quarter 1
findings.headline: LGR Section 24 direction (expected January 2027) will require shadow authority approval for major contracts.
findings.detail: Under Local Government Reorganisation transition arrangements, from January 2027 when the Section 24 order is issued, capital contracts exceeding £1.000m and new revenue contracts above £0.100m will require approval from both the council and the new shadow authority. Officers warn this will impact project approval and procurement processes during the transition period.
findings.matters: Dual-approval requirements will slow procurement and project approval from January 2027 onwards. This creates risk to capital programme delivery and service change initiatives during a period of significant organisational restructuring, when speed and clarity are needed.
findings.figures: Capital contract threshold requiring dual approval: £1.000m. Revenue contract threshold: £0.100m. Section 24 order expected: January 2027.
findings.quote: Under LGR transition arrangements, once the Section 24 order is issued in the New Year (2027), capital contracts over £1.000m and new revenue contracts above £0.100m in value will have to be approved by both the Council and the new shadow authority.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Finance Update - 2026/27 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Additional pay award cost of £0.050m can be absorbed within existing contingency.
findings.detail: The formal local government pay award for 2026/27 has been agreed at 3.3%, compared to the council's budget assumption of 3%, creating an additional cost of approximately £0.050m. This can be met from the £0.500m contingency budget (which had £0.270m remaining after Q1 virements), enabling the council to meet employee obligations without impacting planned service delivery or requiring compensating reductions elsewhere.
findings.matters: While the pay award creates a cost pressure, the council has sufficient contingency reserve to absorb it without service impact. This demonstrates retained budget flexibility. However, contingency funds are finite and are being drawn upon for other pressures.
findings.figures: Pay award cost difference: 3.3% awarded vs 3% budgeted = approximately £0.050m. Original contingency budget: £0.500m. Q1 balance after virements: £0.270m.
findings.quote: The difference between the budgeted pay award and the current offer is estimated to result in an additional cost of approximately £0.050m.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Finance Update - 2026/27 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Investment income forecast to exceed budget by £0.818m (147% better than budgeted).
findings.detail: Investment interest income is forecast at £1.159m against a budget of £0.555m, a favourable variance of £0.818m. The surplus is driven by the council holding higher than anticipated cash balances, which have been invested in well-paying Money Market Funds. General Fund investment income alone contributes £0.637m vs a budget of £0.210m. The forecast surplus is expected to be transferred to reserves.
findings.matters: Strong investment income improves the in-year financial position and helps offset pressures from other areas. However, this surplus reflects higher cash holdings (potentially from S106 and other contributions held on behalf of third parties), not improved operational performance, and should not be assumed to recur.
findings.figures: Total forecast investment income: £1.159m. Budgeted: £0.555m. Variance: £0.818m. General Fund: £0.637m actual vs £0.210m budgeted. HRA: £0.522m vs £0.345m.
findings.quote: Investment interest income is preforming better than budget. Investment income is forecast at £1.159m compared to the budget of £0.555m resulting in a surplus of £0.818m.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Finance Update - 2026/27 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Whitwick Special Expenses remains in forecast deficit despite 50% precept increase.
findings.detail: Whitwick Special Expenses opened 2026/27 with a £20k deficit balance and is forecast to worsen to £21k deficit by year-end, despite the precept being increased by 50% in 2026/27 to help reduce it. The deterioration is driven by reduced cemetery income. Officers note there is limited expenditure that can be deferred, and a review is underway to identify improvement options.
findings.matters: A persistent and worsening deficit in a special expense area, despite aggressive precept increases, suggests underlying structural problems in service costs or delivery that cannot be resolved through pricing. This signals potential service viability issues.
findings.figures: Opening balance (1 April 2026): -£20k. Forecast balance (31 March 2027): -£21k. 2026/27 budget assumed £3.3k contribution to balances; latest forecast is £1k deficit. Precept increased 50% in 2026/27.
findings.quote: Whitwick Special Expenses is forecast to remain in deficit at year-end. The 2026/27 budget included a £3.3k contribution back into balances; however, reduced cemetery income means the latest forecast is a £1k deficit.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Finance Update - 2026/27 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Nearly half the capital programme budget (£16.4m of £34.0m) has been reprofiled into 2027/28.
findings.detail: Of the £33.994m revised capital budget for 2026/27, only £17.583m is forecast to be spent in-year, with £16.412m reprofiled to 2027/28 (48.3% of the budget). Reasons include delays in procurement, scheme design phases not yet complete (Marlborough centre renovation, Moira furnace phase 2), and delays in securing approvals. A period 4 review further increased the reprofiled forecast to £17.387m.
findings.matters: Significant capital reprofiling indicates delays in project delivery and procurement, which signals challenges in project management and delivery capability. For a lender, this affects confidence in the council's capacity to complete capital schemes on planned timescales and realise the intended infrastructure benefits.
findings.figures: Revised capital budget: £33.994m. Q1 forecast outturn: £17.583m. Reprofiled to 2027/28: £16.412m (48.3%). Updated period 4 forecast: £16.625m outturn, £17.387m reprofiled.
findings.quote: £16.412m of the budget is currently expected to be re-profiled to 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Finance Update - 2026/27 Quarter 1
findings.headline: One quarter of planned savings (£0.320m of £1.251m total) are rated at risk of non-delivery.
findings.detail: Of £1.251m in medium-term financial plan savings for 2026/27, £0.258m have been achieved (green status), £0.674m are on track to be achieved (amber), but £0.320m are explicitly rated as at risk of non-delivery (red). This represents 25.6% of the total savings target that may not materialise. Detailed performance against individual proposals is in Appendix 1.
findings.matters: If at-risk savings do not materialise, the council faces a budget deficit of at least £0.320m that will require compensation through reserves drawdown or unplanned service reductions. This directly impacts the council's ability to deliver its spending commitments within available funding.
findings.figures: Total planned savings 2026/27: £1.251m. Achieved (green): £0.258m. On track (amber): £0.674m. At risk (red): £0.320m (25.6% of total).
findings.quote: £0.320m at risk of non-delivery. The performance against detailed proposals is shown in Appendix 1.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Finance Update - 2026/27 Quarter 1
findings.headline: Usable reserves forecast to fall by £16.9m (48%) from £34.9m to £18.1m by year-end.
findings.detail: The council's total usable reserves are forecast to decline from £34.940m at 1 April 2026 to £18.083m at 31 March 2027. The Business Rates reserve alone falls from £18.794m to £1.932m. This represents a forecast draw-down of £16.857m during the year, offset partially by creation of a new £1.000m Legacy Reserve. The paper does not explicitly explain the cause of this large drawdown.
findings.matters: A 48% reduction in reserves in a single year directly affects the council's financial resilience and capacity to absorb future shocks. Lenders assess reserve adequacy as a key indicator of financial sustainability and medium-term financial stability.
findings.figures: Total reserves: £34.940m (opening, 1 April 2026) to £18.083m (forecast, 31 March 2027), a reduction of £16.857m. Business Rates reserve: £18.794m to £1.932m. Service Earmarked Reserves: £6.143m to £5.339m.

findings.paper_title: Marlborough Centre Regeneration Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Lindum Group's bid was approximately £1,000,000 cheaper than the next nearest submission in the competitive mini-competition
findings.detail: The council used a competitive mini-competition between contractors on two construction frameworks to select the PCSA contractor. Lindum had the most competitive overhead and profit and preliminary rates, resulting in a total cost estimate approximately £1,000,000 cheaper than the next nearest submission. Subsequent contracts (enabling and fit-out) are intended to be directly awarded to Lindum via the Pagabo framework.
findings.matters: While initial selection demonstrates cost competitiveness, direct award of subsequent contracts removes competitive tension; however the substantial cost saving on initial selection demonstrates procurement discipline
findings.figures: Lindum cost estimate circa £1,000,000 cheaper than next nearest submission
findings.quote: Of the contractors asked to competitively price the project, Lindum had the most competitive overhead and profit and preliminary rates (such that their cost estimate for the entire project was circa £1,000,000 cheaper than the next nearest submission).

findings.paper_title: Marlborough Centre Regeneration Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Additional planning consent is required due to design changes identified during the detailed design phase
findings.detail: PCSA works identified significant design changes to the designs approved in the November 2024 planning consent. These cumulatively require additional planning consent. The council will submit a new planning application in September 2026, which can be determined while enabling works are underway and before fit-out works commence. Enabling works can proceed under the existing 2024 consent.
findings.matters: Planning delays could delay project completion and create cost pressures; the council is proceeding with enabling works while seeking new consent, creating execution risk if new planning is delayed or refused
findings.figures: Original planning consent November 2024 (reference 22/01823/FULM), new application September 2026
findings.quote: A planning application for these changes will be submitted in September 2026 and can be determined whilst enabling works are underway and before the fit out works commence.

findings.paper_title: Marlborough Centre Regeneration Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Council is accelerating contract awards to complete the project before the Local Government Reorganisation Section 24 Direction takes effect, but the timing of this Direction is unknown
findings.detail: The Section 24 Direction will restrict the council's ability to award contracts over a certain financial value. Announced on 7 September 2026, but the timing of when it will be issued is not yet known. The council is seeking delegated authority now to award contracts before this restriction takes effect, creating time pressure to complete major procurement decisions ahead of an unknown deadline.
findings.matters: Unknown timing of regulatory restrictions creates urgency that could reduce normal procurement discipline and scrutiny; lenders assess whether councils maintain sound financial governance under pressure
findings.figures: Announcement 7 September 2026, Cabinet meeting 22 September 2026, Section 24 Direction timing unknown
findings.quote: At present following the announcement on Monday 7 September it is not yet known when this will happen, however it is prudent to be prepared.

findings.paper_title: Marlborough Centre Regeneration Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Cabinet is delegating authority to award the fit-out works contract without knowing its final price, which is not expected until November
findings.detail: The enabling works estimate of £500,000 is expected just before the Cabinet meeting on 22 September. However, the fit-out works price is not expected until November, yet the report seeks delegated authority to award this contract (subject to cost remaining within budget and discussion with the Leader). This allows contract award without returning to Cabinet for formal decision once the price is known.
findings.matters: Delegating authority to award contracts before final pricing is known creates risk that actual costs exceed expectations; lenders need to understand whether major contracts are awarded with full cost certainty
findings.figures: Enabling works estimate £500,000 expected 22 September, fit-out works price expected November
findings.quote: The fit out works cost is expected in November. To maintain the desired project delivery programme it is proposed that this figure will be discussed with the Leader Of The council before award of contract (subject to delegation of authority requested in this paper).

findings.paper_title: Marlborough Centre Regeneration Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Project budget increased by £2,400,000 in February 2026, a 54% increase from the August 2021 approval

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - 2026/27 Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to grow 28% to £106.7m
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement (measuring cumulative outstanding debt finance) is forecast to grow from £83.2m (31.03.2026) to £106.7m (31.03.2029), an increase of £23.5m over three years. The growth is driven primarily by HRA capital investment, whilst General Fund CFR decreases from £33.6m to £30.2m. Current debt stands at £51–54m, with the CFR-debt gap funded from capital receipts and other sources.
findings.matters: Growing debt obligations require future revenue resources to service; lenders assess sustainability and whether remaining borrowing capacity is adequate.
findings.quote: The Authority's cumulative outstanding amount of debt finance is measured by the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR). This increases with new debt-financed capital expenditure and reduces with MRP (loans fund repayments) and capital receipts used to replace debt.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 - 2026/27 Prudential Indicators
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account financing costs forecast to jump from 4% to 16% of net revenue
findings.detail: HRA financing costs are forecast to fall to £1.0m (4% of net revenue) in 2026/27, then rise sharply to £2.7m (14%) in 2027/28 and £3.2m (16%) in 2028/29. This doubling of the proportion of HRA net revenue consumed by debt servicing represents a structural revenue pressure emerging in 2027/28 driven by HRA capital investment in housing stock (£17.9m), new homes (£5.9m), and fleet replacement (£3.1m).
findings.matters: Rising HRA financing costs constrain housing investment or require rent increases; lenders assess whether service sustainability is at risk.
findings.quote: Housing Revenue Account Net Financing costs (£'m): 2026/27 forecast 1.0, 2027/28 budget 2.7, 2028/29 budget 3.2; Proportion of net revenue stream: 2026/27 forecast 4%, 2027/28 budget 14%, 2028/29 budget 16%

The 2026/27 programme includes major regeneration initiatives: Marlborough Centre purchase and renovation (£2.7m), Enterprise Park (£3.7m), Stenson Square public realm (£2.0m), and Coalville regeneration (£2.6m).

findings.headline: Unit 4 finance system unable to automate rent reconciliation after 2+ years, stuck in testing
findings.detail: A 2022/23 recommendation for automated weekly rent uploads from housing system to general ledger (to enable reconciliation) was due August 2023. As of June 2026 it remains incomplete: the process is 'currently being tested' with no resolution date. This has been extended seven times citing 'Issues with Unit 4.' Weekly reconciliation is a basic financial control.
findings.matters: Finance system non-functionality indicates unresolved technical issues in the core accounting system; 2+ year delay signals project management or technical capacity problems; lack of weekly reconciliation increases misstatement risk in housing revenue.
findings.figures: Originally due Aug-23; currently Jun-26; seven extensions across 33 months
findings.quote: With the introduction of Unit 4 (new Finance System) the rent debit should be uploaded automatically from the Housing System to the General Ledger each week. Due to issues with Unit4 it has not yet been possible to implement this recommendation.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Internal Audit Progress Report (Q1)
findings.headline: Asbestos management function paralysed by staffing crisis for 18+ months with exposure to unlimited HSE fines
findings.detail: Recommendations from 2023/24 remain unimplemented as of August 2026 (originally due November 2024). The asset team is missing two managers on long-term sick leave, cannot fill three crucial posts, and has one critical role carried by unqualified staff. The audit states that quality assurance is at risk and the failure to manage exposes the council to HSE prosecution with unlimited fines. The service is now considering outsourcing the entire function.
findings.matters: Represents unquantified material liability exposure from regulatory breach; indicates management capacity failure; outsourcing consideration shows loss of internal control.
findings.figures: Two managers absent long-term sick; three posts unfilled; recommendations 18–20 months overdue; multiple extensions from Nov-24 through Aug-26
findings.quote: Quality assurance is at risk due to insufficient administration of the asbestos data and as a consequence puts operatives, contractors, staff and other end users at risk. Failure to manage properly exposes NWLDC to prosecution from the Regulator, HSE and leading to unlimited fines.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Opinion Audit and Governance Committee Report
findings.headline: Further embedding of improvements required across the council
findings.detail: Although management has responded with action plans and some progress has been made, the audit concludes that 'further work is required to ensure that improvements are fully embedded and consistently applied across the Council' and to ensure improvements become 'part of day-to-day operations'.
findings.matters: Inconsistency in applying controls across the organisation indicates that improvements are not yet institutional, creating ongoing governance and control risk.

findings.quote: further work is required to ensure that improvements are fully embedded and consistently applied across the Council

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Opinion Audit and Governance Committee Report
findings.headline: Control weaknesses reported in previous years remain unresolved
findings.detail: The limited assurance reflects not new issues but the persistence of control weaknesses identified in prior-year audits. The report states these have 'not yet been fully addressed', indicating slow or incomplete remediation of known problems across multiple years.
findings.matters: Recurring unresolved audit findings suggest systemic issues or management capacity constraints in implementing controls, and raise questions about the timeline and pace of remediation.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: issues reported in previous years that have not yet been fully addressed

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Opinion Audit and Governance Committee Report
findings.headline: Annual internal audit conclusion is Limited Assurance
findings.detail: The Internal Audit Manager has concluded that the council's overall framework for governance, risk management and internal control merits only Limited Assurance. This reflects significant control weaknesses identified in key areas, not merely that improvements are in progress.
findings.matters: A limited assurance opinion signals material governance and internal control weaknesses that affect the council's financial and operational resilience, and will be material to lender assessment of management capability.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: the Annual Internal Audit Conclusion for 2025/26 is one of Limited Assurance

findings.paper_title: External Audit - Building Back Assurance Audit and Governance Committee Report
findings.headline: Statutory backstop deadline of 31 January 2027 for 2025/26 audit completion creates pressure point for audit recovery
findings.detail: Government has introduced statutory backstop dates requiring auditors to issue reports by specified deadlines even where planned procedures are incomplete. For 2025/26, this deadline is 31 January 2027. The council must achieve full audit assurance restoration within this timeframe or face a fifth consecutive year of qualified audit opinion.
findings.matters: The deadline creates a hard constraint on the Building Back Assurance programme. If the programme fails to restore full assurance by January 2027, the council will have no choice but to issue another disclaimer, perpetuating governance and financial reporting uncertainty.
findings.figures: 31 January 2027
findings.quote: For 2025/26, the statutory backstop date is 31 January 2027.

findings.paper_title: External Audit - Building Back Assurance Audit and Governance Committee Report
findings.headline: Four consecutive years of disclaimer audit opinions for financial years 2021/22 through 2024/25
findings.detail: The predecessor auditor issued disclaimer opinions for 2021/22 and 2022/23; the current auditor Azets issued disclaimers for 2023/24 and 2024/25. This means the council's Statement of Accounts has lacked full audit assurance for four years, requiring rebuilding of assurance over opening balances and historic transactions.
findings.matters: Disclaimer audit opinions indicate the auditor cannot form a view on whether accounts are fairly stated. For lenders, this signals uncertainty over the council's actual financial position and governance strength; for finance directors, it reflects a significant failure in financial reporting reliability.
findings.quote: The predecessor auditor issued disclaimer opinions for the financial years 2021/22 and 2022/23. Disclaimer opinions were also issued by Azets for 2023/24 and 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Treasury Management Activity Report Q1 updated with Inv Benchmarking
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement rising sharply, driven by HRA growth
findings.detail: Total CFR forecast to rise from £83.22m (actual) to £90.31m (2026/27) to £101.1m (2027/28) and £107.3m (2028/29). The majority of growth is in HRA (rising from £49.60m to £57.85m immediately). General Fund CFR is projected to decline.
findings.matters: Rapid CFR growth, especially in HRA, indicates the council has committed to substantial capital investment programmes. As CFR rises while external borrowing falls, the debt service burden shifts increasingly onto internal resources and MRP, reducing flexibility.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Treasury Management Activity Report Q1 updated with Inv Benchmarking
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio acts as constraint on future borrowing capacity
findings.detail: The council holds £9.9m of directly owned property and land purchased before CIPFA code restrictions on borrowing for yield. It states it will review options for exiting these investments before undertaking further additional borrowing. These investments are forecast to generate £320k income in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Non-productive assets held in advance of CIPFA restrictions create a decision point before the council can increase borrowing: the council must first decide whether to liquidate or retain £9.9m of property. This restricts flexibility and signals the council views its current asset base as partly constrained.
findings.figures: Commercial property investments £9.9m; forecast income £320k; all located within the district
findings.quote: Before undertaking further additional borrowing the Council will review the options for exiting these investments.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Treasury Management Activity Report Q1 updated with Inv Benchmarking
findings.headline: HRA capital programme requiring £9.7m borrowing has been deferred, shifted to internal borrowing instead
findings.detail: The council forecast £9.7m of new external borrowing for the HRA in 2026/27 but has undertaken none so far. This has resulted in an equal increase in internal borrowing. The HRA CFR is rising from £49.60m to £57.85m by year end.
findings.matters: Deferral of planned borrowing can signal cash pressure or capital programme slippage; shifting to internal borrowing depletes the council's liquidity buffer and removes a mechanism to fund growing capital needs, especially in the HRA where growth is accelerating.
findings.figures: Forecast new HRA borrowing £9.7m; actual to date £0m; HRA CFR rising to £57.85m (from £49.60m); internal borrowing forecast to rise from £29.43m to £37.84m
findings.quote: The Authority was forecast to undertake new borrowing of £9.7m for the HRA in the 2026/27 financial year, however, none has so far been undertaken. There has therefore been an equal increase in the internal borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Treasury Management Activity Report Q1 updated with Inv Benchmarking
findings.headline: Council is over-borrowed relative to liability benchmark with little room for adjustment
findings.detail: The council currently holds £53.8m of external borrowing against a liability benchmark requirement of £33.0m. The liability benchmark analysis states the council is likely to have no external borrowing requirement in 2026/27 but acknowledges little room for adjustment and that the situation may evolve to create a borrowing requirement in the next couple of years.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has headroom to absorb adverse changes—cash shortfalls, accelerated capital spending, or investment losses—without coming back to the market in distress.
findings.figures: External borrowing £53.8m; liability benchmark requirement £33.0m; forecast liability benchmark £39.3m (2026/27), £43.7m (2027/28), £44.0m (2028/29)
findings.quote: This graph demonstrates that by using internal resources the Council is likely to not have an external borrowing requirement in 2026/27. However, there is little room for adjustment and the Liability Benchmark graph is an estimate and subject to significant change. This situation may evolve and create a borrowing requirement in the next couple of years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: External auditors identified underlying procurement failures and inadequate cost monitoring for Unit4
findings.detail: Azets flagged that there were 'underlying issues' with Unit4 procurement and 'monitoring and reporting of system costs could have been more robust.' The Audit and Governance Committee has formally requested further detail from officers and statutory officers on this matter.
findings.matters: Procurement governance failure on core financial infrastructure indicates control gaps that could extend to other supplier contracts and capital commitments.
findings.figures: Audit and Governance Committee formal request for detail on procurement issues
findings.quote: The Council acknowledges the comments made by the external auditors regarding the procurement of the finance system, specifically noting that there were underlying issues and that monitoring and reporting of system costs could have been more robust. In response, the Audit and Governance Committee has formally requested further detail on these matters.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Unit4 finance system implementation ongoing; control environment and key reconciliations remain weak
findings.detail: The Unit4 finance system 'has continued to require significant management attention' in 2025/26. The council identified 'the need to further strengthen elements of the control environment (including key reconciliations, system administration and the pace of implementing related audit recommendations).' A security audit identified weaknesses in system administration. The council has changed implementation partners effective December 2025 and procured external specialist Vision ERP to conduct comprehensive review.
findings.matters: Persistent weaknesses in core financial system controls directly affect the accuracy and reliability of financial reporting and transaction processing that lenders depend on for due diligence.
findings.figures: New support/maintenance provider commenced December 2025; Vision ERP review commissioned; budget allocated in 2026/27 for further enhancements
findings.quote: Key area of focus in 2025/26: the implementation and ongoing operation of the Unit4 finance system has continued to require significant management attention. The annual review identified the need to further strengthen elements of the control environment (including key reconciliations, system administration and the pace of implementing related audit recommendations). This remains a priority in our governance improvement plan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Accounts approval missed statutory backstop date by 12 days
findings.detail: The Audit and Governance Committee approved the 2024/25 Statement of Accounts on 26 February 2026 (the statutory deadline), but the acting Chair did not sign them. The accounts were then approved and signed at a reconvened Committee meeting on 10 March 2026, 12 days after the backstop date. The council is working with external auditors to meet the 2025/26 backstop date of January 2027.
findings.matters: Failure to meet statutory deadlines for financial reporting indicates process breakdowns in the accounts close cycle and raises questions about whether the council can deliver timely financial statements.
findings.figures: 26 February 2026 (backstop date); 10 March 2026 (actual signature)
findings.quote: Although the Audit and Governance Committee approved the accounts on 26 February 2026, the acting Chair did not sign them following the meeting. The Statement of Accounts were therefore approved and signed at a reconvened Committee meeting on 10 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Finance team capacity severely constrained, limiting audit access and preventing timely budget setting
findings.detail: Auditors report finance team had 'severely constrained' capacity to engage with the audit due to need to prioritise production of 2024/25 accounts and annual budget setting. This prevented auditors obtaining responses to queries in a timely manner and contributed to incomplete audit work.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity problems prevent both the council and auditors from doing their jobs effectively. For a lender, this signals ongoing risk of continued late reporting, errors remaining undetected, and insufficient management attention to financial governance and forecasting.
findings.figures: Capacity constraint documented in audit report affecting 2024/25 audit
findings.quote: The finance team responded to our audit queries to the best of their ability. However, their capacity to engage was severely constrained by the need to prioritise the production of the 2024/25 accounts and the annual budget setting process.

findings.paper_title: Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Potential material adjustments to property, plant and equipment identified but will not be processed until 2025/26 accounts
findings.detail: Auditors began rebuilding assurance over PPE movements (additions, disposals, reclassifications, depreciation) across all disclaimed years. Work is ongoing and has already identified 'material adjustments' to the accounts, but these cannot be processed into the current year statements due to time constraints.
findings.matters: Material PPE adjustments remaining unresolved after audit means the council's asset position may be overstated or understated by amounts large enough to matter. For a lender assessing collateral or debt capacity, unresolved material adjustments create valuation uncertainty.
findings.figures: Material adjustments identified; work ongoing on 2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25
findings.quote: Work completed to date has identified some material adjustments, however we will not know the full extent of these until we have finished our build back testing on PPE movements. Any adjustments to the financial statements will be processed within the 2025/26 statement of accounts.

findings.paper_title: Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Council classified as 'higher risk' requiring full assurance rebuild over four years of unaudited income and expenditure
findings.detail: Auditors completed a risk assessment under LARRIG 06 and classified North West Leicestershire as higher risk due to timeliness of accounts production, disclaimed periods, control environment, changes in finance personnel, and complexity of reserves. As a result, auditors are undertaking four-year rebuild of assurance on PPE, housing benefit, and other service expenditure, with work still in progress.
findings.matters: Higher-risk classification and ongoing build-back work indicate structural problems in financial management and controls. For a lender, this means assurance over the council's true financial position will remain incomplete until 2027/28 at the earliest, creating prolonged uncertainty.
findings.figures: Build-back work spans 2021/22 to 2024/25 (four years); assessment: higher end of risk spectrum
findings.quote: From the above work, we assessed North Leicestershire District Council at the higher end of the risk spectrum. This indicates that we are required to gain full assurance over the income and expenditure balances for all missing years of assurance.

findings.paper_title: Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Unit 4 financial system implementation failed to meet requirements and created account production delays
findings.detail: The council implemented Unit4 accounting software on 01 April 2023. Auditors found no disaster recovery or business continuity plan for the system. The implementation caused 'a number of issues' making routine financial management tasks difficult and resulted in delays producing the 2023/24 statements. Council was unable to provide evidence of risk assessment before or during implementation.
findings.matters: A major accounting system implementation that has failed to deliver on time and continues to cause operational problems is a material governance failure. For a lender, this suggests either poor vendor selection, inadequate internal capability, or both—increasing risk of future service disruption and control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Go-live 01 April 2023; 2023/24 accounts delayed; no disaster recovery plan in place
findings.quote: The Council has implemented a new financial accounting system (Unit4) which went live on 01 April 2023. We have been made aware that a number of issues have occurred since the system has been in place which have made performing routine financial management tasks difficult. The implementation of the new system has also resulted in delays of the production of the 2023/24 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Three significant weaknesses in governance arrangements, including Unit 4 system implementation and finance team capacity
findings.detail: Auditors identified three significant weaknesses: (1) council unable to produce documentation supporting Unit 4 procurement decisions or risk assessment; (2) finance team capacity restricted prevented timely production of accounts; (3) reporting to members did not communicate severity and extent of Unit4 issues. The auditors state they are not satisfied the council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
findings.matters: Significant governance weaknesses in a major system implementation and financial reporting processes indicate weaker internal controls and oversight. For a lender, this signals elevated risk of future financial reporting problems and poor decision-making on major capital commitments.
findings.figures: Three statutory significant weaknesses identified; Unit4 went live 01 April 2023
findings.quote: We have concluded there are significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.paper_title: Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Draft accounts delivered 7 months late, over 200 days after statutory deadline
findings.detail: The Accounts and Audit Regulations 2015 require draft financial statements by 31 May 2025. North West Leicestershire delivered them on 16 January 2026. The auditors rate the quality and timeliness RED, noting this created insufficient time to complete planned testing and contributed directly to the disclaimer decision.
findings.matters: Late accounts prevent timely lender assessment and damage governance transparency. A five-month delay suggests serious capacity or system problems within the finance function, both risk factors for lenders.
findings.figures: Deadline 31 May 2025; delivery 16 January 2026 (230 days late)
findings.quote: Under The Accounts and Audit Regulations 2015, the deadline for the production and approval for the draft financial statements was 31 May 2025. The Council did not prepare its draft accounts in line with this deadline. The draft financial statements were published and made available for inspection on the Council's website on 16 January 2026, over seven months after the statutory deadline.

findings.paper_title: Audit Completion Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Auditors will disclaim opinion on 2024/25 accounts due to four consecutive years of unaudited balances
findings.detail: The council has received disclaimed audit opinions for 2021/22, 2022/23, and 2023/24. The 2024/25 audit cannot be completed to support an unmodified opinion because the auditors lack sufficient assurance over opening balances in key areas and have been unable to test all transactions occurring during the disclaimed years. This means the financial statements cannot be relied upon.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assess the council's true financial position or whether reserves are materially misstated. A finance director cannot rely on the accounts for decision-making. This is the most severe audit outcome and signals deep control and reporting problems.
findings.figures: Four consecutive years disclaimed (2021/22, 2022/23, 2023/24, plus 2024/25)
findings.quote: Due to the challenges of undertaking an audit where the previous four years have been disclaimed, combined with the late receipt of the draft statement of accounts on the 16 January 2026, it has not been possible for us to undertake sufficient work to regain full assurance and support an unmodified audit opinion ahead of the backstop date of 27 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: 2024/25 Provisional Financial Outturn - General Fund Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Vehicle procurement delays creating both capital slippage and forcing operational spending on expensive hiring workarounds
findings.detail: Fleet Replacement Programme reprofiled £5.3m (93% of budget) and Food Waste Rollout slipped full £1.2m budget both due to long lead times on vehicle purchases. Concurrently, Waste Services incurred £104k unbudgeted vehicle hire costs to cover the delayed procurements, showing supply chain constraints forcing costly operational workarounds.
findings.matters: Supply chain bottlenecks are preventing capital investment delivery while creating unplanned operational costs, indicating forward-looking execution risk
findings.figures: £5.3m Fleet reprofiled, £1.2m Food Waste slipped, £104k additional hire costs
findings.quote: The Food Waste Rollout Programme slipped its full budget allocation of £1.2m into future years due to delays in the procurement process which are due to the long lead in times on vehicle purchases.

findings.paper_title: 2024/25 Provisional Financial Outturn - General Fund Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Two of six Special Expenses accounts in deficit at year-end, with precept increases planned to recover shortfalls
findings.detail: Special Expenses outturn shows £32k overspend. While the overall Special Expenses reserve increased to £84k, two of the six service-area accounts remain in deficit. The council will increase precepts through the annual budget process to recover these deficits.
findings.matters: Service-level deficits requiring precept increases indicate specific areas unable to manage costs or balance budgets
findings.figures: £32k overspend, 2 of 6 accounts in deficit, Special Expenses reserve £84k
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2025, two accounts were in deficit, while the remaining four held balances above the minimum threshold. For those Special Expense accounts in deficit, precepts will be increased through the annual budget process to recover the shortfall.

findings.paper_title: 2024/25 Provisional Financial Outturn - General Fund Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Multiple directorates overspent on agency staffing due to persistent recruitment difficulties and vacancies
findings.detail: Chief Executive directorate overspent £173k on higher-than-budgeted agency costs in Legal due to recruitment difficulties requiring continued specialist temporary support. Community Services Waste Services faced £333k pressure from sickness and vacancies requiring agency staffing. Place Directorate also experienced agency cost pressures from ongoing recruitment challenges.
findings.matters: Persistent staffing cost pressures across multiple services suggest structural labour market constraints and ongoing cost control risks
findings.figures: Chief Executive £173k overspend, Community Services Waste £333k, Finance staffing £257k above budget
findings.quote: This adverse variance was driven primarily by staffing and operational pressures, most notably higher‑than‑budgeted agency costs within Legal arising from recruitment difficulties that required the continued use of temporary specialist support throughout the year.

findings.paper_title: 2024/25 Provisional Financial Outturn - General Fund Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Capital programme achieved only 24% delivery rate, with £13.2m underspend driven by procurement delays and project slippage
findings.detail: The £17.5m capital budget delivered only £4.3m in actual spend. Major slippages include Fleet Replacement (£5.3m of £5.7m budget), Food Waste Rollout (£1.2m full budget), Disabled Facilities (£2.4m of £3m), and Coalville regeneration (£0.8m). The council attributes most slippage to procurement process delays and long lead times.
findings.matters: Significant capital underperformance indicates execution risk on planned investments and delays to planned service improvements
findings.figures: £17.5m budget, £4.3m outturn, £13.2m underspend, 24% spend rate
findings.quote: The revised General Fund capital budget for 2024/2025 was £17.5m, with a final outturn of £4.3m, representing 24% of the approved programme. This resulted in an underspend of £13.2m, of which most is proposed to be reprofiled into future years.

findings.paper_title: 2024/45 Provisional Financial Outturn - Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Cabinet Report
findings.headline: £4.9m reported revenue surplus is artificial; driven by £4.0m in deferred capital and reserve contributions, not operational strength
findings.detail: The £4.9m underspend (improvement from £1.7m Q3 forecast) was almost entirely driven by £4.0m in planned appropriations not being required: £2.5m planned transfer to reserves and £1.5m revenue contribution to capital were cancelled due to capital programme slippage. This means the surplus exists because planned investment and reserve-building did not happen, masking the council's true operational position.
findings.matters: The HRA has a £4.0m backlog of deferred capital maintenance and reserve funding that will need to be caught up; this represents future cash flow pressure and indicates the current year's surplus is a timing anomaly, not a sign of financial strength
findings.figures: £4.9m total underspend; £4.0m from cancelled appropriations (£2.5m reserves + £1.5m capital contribution); represents 82% of the reported surplus
findings.quote: Appropriations were £4.0m lower than budgeted with a £2.5m transfer to reserves and a £1.5m revenue contribution towards capital spending not taking place. Contributions to capital spend were not required due to capital slippage, resulting in lower‑than‑anticipated expenditure during the financial year.

findings.paper_title: 2024/45 Provisional Financial Outturn - Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Asset impairment and disposal losses of £1.039m indicate housing stock condition is deteriorating faster than anticipated
findings.detail: Operating expenditure overran by £331k partly due to £852k overspend on depreciation and impairment of fixed assets, combined with an unbudgeted £187k loss on the sale of HRA fixed assets. These non-cash charges signal that the housing stock's condition is being reassessed downward, requiring higher depreciation charges and realising losses on asset disposals.
findings.matters: Accelerating asset impairments indicate the council's housing stock requires more investment than assumed to maintain; this affects future capital planning and the sustainability of the asset base underpinning the HRA
findings.figures: £852k overspend on depreciation and impairment; £187k unbudgeted loss on asset sales; total non-cash charges £1.039m
findings.quote: an overspend of £852k on Depreciation and Impairment of Fixed Assets, [and] an unbudgeted loss of £187k on the sale of HRA fixed assets and £8k in unbudgeted debt management expenses.

findings.paper_title: 2024/45 Provisional Financial Outturn - Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Dwelling rent income fell £565k short of budget, reducing core HRA revenue by 2.7%
findings.detail: Actual dwelling rent was £565k below the £21.3m budgeted for the year. While higher service charges (+£735k) and other income (+£222k) offset this gap at year-end, the core rental income shortfall raises questions about occupancy rates, void management, or rent levels versus assumption. For a council with social housing borrowing, rental income stability is critical.
findings.matters: Dwelling rent is the primary revenue stream for servicing HRA debt; a 2.7% miss signals either occupancy problems, collection weakness, or inability to achieve forecast rent levels, each of which erodes debt service capacity
findings.figures: Dwelling rent £565k below budget (shortfall on £21.3m base = 2.7%); offset by service charges +£735k
findings.quote: Lower‑than‑expected dwelling rent (£565k below budget) was more than offset by increases in other income streams, comprising higher service charges (+£735k) and higher other income (+£222k).

findings.paper_title: 2024/45 Provisional Financial Outturn - Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Cabinet Report
findings.headline: HRA capital programme delivered only 39% of budget; 68% slippage driven by in-house capacity constraints
findings.detail: The capital programme outturn was £7.6m against a £19.4m revised budget, with £13.2m (68%) of scheduled spending slipped into future years. The Home Improvement Programme alone carried £8.2m slippage, with £3.423m attributable specifically to capacity constraints within the in-house team. The council has since engaged an external contractor to enhance delivery capacity, indicating inability to meet planned investment schedules.
findings.matters: A council unable to deliver half its planned capital budget signals operational and governance weaknesses; deferred maintenance backlogs create future cash flow pressure and may require accelerated borrowing to catch up
findings.figures: £19.436m revised budget vs £7.586m outturn (39% delivery rate); £13.209m total slippage; £3.423m slippage in Home Improvement alone due to capacity
findings.quote: £3,423k across all other projects due to capacity constraints within the in-house team. An external contractor has been subsequently engaged to enhance overall delivery capacity.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Robustness of Budget Estimates Council Report
findings.headline: Finance system implementation delays persist; reporting improvements not yet complete
findings.detail: The council implemented a new financial system in April 2023 to improve reporting capability. However, the finance teams remain behind schedule in catching up from implementation delays. The council is planning training for all budget holders and working with a new supplier for system support and maintenance.
findings.matters: Ongoing delays in financial system implementation suggest the council's reporting and control environment is not yet fully stable. Combined with the limited audit assurance opinion, this indicates the financial management function is still in transition and not operating at full efficiency.
findings.figures: System implementation: April 2023; Current status as of February 2026: catching up on implementation delays
findings.quote: The Council implemented a new financial system in April 2023 to improve its reporting. Enhancements to the system have been made, however, the Finance Teams are still catching up on delays caused by the system implementation.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Robustness of Budget Estimates Council Report
findings.headline: No business rates pooling income in 2026/27 after reset; previous growth advantage removed
findings.detail: Between 2013/14 and 2025/26, the council benefited from local business rates pooling arrangements that allowed retention of growth. The 2026/27 business rates reset raises the baseline and eliminates available growth, removing the pooling advantage. The council expects no business rates pools in England in 2026/27.
findings.matters: This removes a discretionary income source the council has previously relied on. It represents a structural income loss that must be offset by other funding, savings, or service reduction.
findings.figures: Business rates pool arrangements: 2013/14–2025/26 active; 2026/27 onwards: none expected
findings.quote: It is expected there will be no business rates pools in England in 2026/27. This view has been backed by the Council's external advisors, with MHCLG also expecting no pools.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Robustness of Budget Estimates Council Report
findings.headline: No new capital borrowing; strategy relies on business rates reserve depletion
findings.detail: The council has explicitly chosen not to borrow new money for the capital programme beyond 2023/24 approvals. The £18.3m capital funding comes from government grants (£4.8m), business rates reserve depletion (£13.2m), and revenue contributions (£324k). This strategy avoids future revenue pressure from interest and repayment costs but depletes financial flexibility.
findings.matters: While avoiding future revenue pressure from borrowing, this strategy depletes reserves and limits flexibility for future investment or emergencies. For lenders, it indicates the council is prioritising reserve preservation over capital investment capacity, suggesting a tighter cash position than headline figures indicate.
findings.figures: Capital funding 2026/27: government grants £4.8m, business rates reserve £13.2m, revenue £324k; Business Rates Reserve balance 31/3/27: £11,074k
findings.quote: No new borrowing, over and above that approved in the 2023/24 budget, is proposed to fund the capital programme. This is to ensure the Council does not create additional revenue pressures in the future arising from interest and capital repayment costs.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Robustness of Budget Estimates Council Report
findings.headline: HRA operating surplus declining: down £800k year-on-year to £2.028m in 2026/27
findings.detail: The HRA operating position is deteriorating. The 2026/27 operating surplus is £2,028k, a decline of £800k from 2025/26. This trajectory continues downward to £1,850k in 2027/28 and £1,725k in 2028/29. Declining surplus reduces the HRA's capacity for capital investment and debt repayment without external borrowing.
findings.matters: A declining HRA surplus indicates reduced financial headroom for the 30-year housing business plan. The council is dependent on this surplus to fund capital work and contribute to debt repayment. Deterioration signals reduced capacity to absorb pressures or invest in housing stock.
findings.quote: The HRA budget for 2026/27 shows an operating surplus of £2,028k. This is an £800k decrease from 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Robustness of Budget Estimates Council Report
findings.headline: External audit opinion currently at 'limited assurance' level, not reasonable assurance
findings.detail: The council's current external audit opinion is 'limited assurance' rather than the desired 'reasonable assurance'. The council has identified this as a governance gap and lists improvement of the audit opinion as a specific action in its mitigation plan.
findings.matters: Limited assurance indicates gaps in control or governance that auditors have identified. For lenders, this represents control weakness that warrants monitoring and increases the risk profile of the authority.
findings.figures: Current audit opinion: limited assurance (target: reasonable assurance)
findings.quote: Continue to review and improve the Council's governance arrangements with a focus on improving the annual audit opinion to reasonable assurance from the current limited assurance.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Robustness of Budget Estimates Council Report
findings.headline: HRA capital programme delivery risk on £22.6m spend flagged as ambitious
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is planning £22.6m of capital spending in 2026/27, which the council acknowledges is ambitious relative to previous delivery. The Housing Improvement Programme is specifically identified as the highest-risk area for delivery delays. Slippage would affect revenue pressure and the council's capacity to fund the 30-year housing debt repayment plan.
findings.matters: HRA borrowing repayment capacity is critical to council creditworthiness. Delays in capital delivery indicate slippage against the funding plan and affect the council's ability to execute its 30-year business plan to repay self-financing debt by 2042.
findings.figures: HRA Capital Programme: £22.6m in 2026/27; HRA borrowing from 2012 self-financing initiative to be repaid by 2042
findings.quote: The HRA Capital Programme is planned to spend £22.6m in 2026/27. Based on previous years' experience this is an ambitious level of estimated spend. The area of the capital programme at greatest risk of delay is the Housing Improvement Programme.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Robustness of Budget Estimates Council Report
findings.headline: Significant funding 'cliff edge' when transitional support ends in 2028/29
findings.detail: The council benefits from a multi-year settlement through 2028/29, but a substantial portion of 2028/29 funding is transitional. This support will be withdrawn after 2028/29, resulting in a material reduction in funding. The council must rebuild business rates growth during 2026–2029 to sustain services beyond the settlement period.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the medium-term financial trajectory. A cliff-edge funding drop represents material refinancing risk and potential need for service reductions or additional borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £34.3m funding; 2027/28: £34.2m funding; 2028/29: £34.1m funding (then transitional funding withdrawn)
findings.quote: A substantial proportion of the Council's funding in the 2028/29 financial year is transitional, and this support will be withdrawn after that year, resulting in a significant 'cliff edge' reduction in funding.

This decline means the council must rely increasingly on borrowing and capital receipts, indicating either finite reserve availability or constrained revenue capacity to support capital investment.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account financing costs escalating to 16% of revenue stream by 2028/29

findings.matters: Rising financing costs constrain HRA capacity for stock maintenance and reserve building. At 16% of revenue, little headroom remains for unexpected costs or income volatility.

findings.headline: General Fund capital borrowing increasing 411% in one year as policy shifts from no new borrowing
findings.detail: The council's financing plan shows debt as a capital funding source jumping from £1.9m (2025/26) to £9.7m (2026/27). This represents a significant departure from the council's stated policy (Section 4.3) of no new borrowing to fund General Fund capital investments since 2023/24, signalling a shift in capital strategy.
findings.matters: Sharp increases in capital borrowing increase debt service costs and Minimum Revenue Provision charges on future revenue budgets, constraining financial flexibility.

findings.matters: A council with a track record of missing capital project deadlines poses execution risk. Slippage increases financing costs; cost overruns erode financial reserves.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget and Rent Setting Council Report
findings.headline: Finance system implementation in April 2023 continues to cause reporting delays, affecting accounts sign-off and indicating control weaknesses.
findings.detail: The budget risk assessment notes that the Finance Teams 'are still catching up on delays caused by the system implementation' nearly three years after go-live. Statements of Accounts for 2023/24 were not signed off until August 2025, and 2024/25 until January 2026 (both published at backstop deadline). The assessment identifies the need for a new supplier to 'enhance the reporting arrangements', suggesting current system support is inadequate.
findings.matters: Ongoing reporting delays represent a control and audit weakness. Delayed accounts sign-off limits the reliability and timeliness of financial information available to decision-makers and lenders. The need for supplier changes indicates unresolved system stability issues.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget and Rent Setting Council Report
findings.headline: Total capital reserves forecast to decline by £1.2m (6.6%) from £18.2m to £17.0m over the three-year MTFP period.
findings.detail: Capital reserves (Major Repairs Reserve, Capital Receipts, and Debt Repayment Reserve) are forecast to fall from £18.184m at 31/03/2026 to £16.971m at 31/03/2028. This declining trajectory reflects the shifting balance away from self-funded capital investment toward external borrowing. The reserve depletion accelerates in 2027/28 when capital receipts drop sharply (from £5.6m to £1.9m by 2028/29).
findings.matters: Declining capital self-funding capacity increases dependency on external borrowing to deliver the £66.6m three-year capital programme. This constrains the council's ability to respond to future capital priorities or maintain capital spending if borrowing becomes more expensive.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget and Rent Setting Council Report
findings.headline: Council cannot refinance debt despite acknowledging it would be beneficial, because local government reorganisation creates succession risk for successor authorities.
findings.detail: The budget documents that early repayment of loans would trigger 'significant lender premiums' creating 'an immediate and material cost pressure', but also that 'Sensitivity analysis demonstrates that full repayment of all maturity loans would result in a substantial and unsustainable resource shortfall.' The council has chosen not to refinance, explicitly citing uncertainty about local government reorganisation expected before the next loan maturity in 2036/37. This blocks a potential financial solution that might otherwise address the tightening reserve position.
findings.matters: Financial flexibility is constrained by reorganisation uncertainty. The council is locked into its current debt structure despite it potentially limiting capital investment capacity and forcing reliance on external borrowing.
findings.figures: Next loan maturity £10m in 2036/37, expected local government reorganisation before that date
findings.quote: The Council's current financial modelling assumes that maturity loans are held to term, as early repayment would trigger significant lender premiums, creating an immediate and material cost pressure with no corresponding financial benefit.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget and Rent Setting Council Report
findings.headline: HRA working balance held at exactly the minimum threshold of £1m with no headroom, and the minimum level itself is noted as requiring review.
findings.detail: The budget forecasts maintain the HRA working balance at £1m (approximately 4.4% of the £22.7m revenue budget) across all three years 2026/27 to 2028/29. This is at the stated minimum level, leaving zero buffer. The risk assessment notes this minimum 'is to be reviewed as part of the HRA business planning process', suggesting the current minimum may be reconsidered, potentially putting further pressure on reserves if it increases.
findings.matters: Zero reserve headroom creates vulnerability to any revenue shortfall (voids, arrears) or unexpected cost pressure (emergency repairs, compliance). A housing account with £22m+ revenue holding only £1m minimum contingency is tight and leaves no flexibility.
findings.figures: HRA Reserve £1m (constant 2026/27-2028/29), minimum level currently subject to review
findings.quote: The Council has a minimum level of reserves for HRA (£1m). This level is to be reviewed as part of the HRA business planning process.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Budget and Rent Setting Council Report
findings.headline: External borrowing requirement increases by £12.6m over the next three years, reaching £30.8m total at 5.3% interest rate.
findings.detail: The HRA capital programme is increasingly funded by external borrowing rather than reserves. The budget explicitly states the increase in borrowing is 'due to decreased usage of reserves to fund projects'. At the assumed interest rate of 5.3% (elevated by historical standards), this represents additional annual debt service costs rising from existing levels. This accelerates the HRA's shift from self-funded capital (reserves-based) to externally-financed (borrowing-based).
findings.matters: Increased borrowing reduces financial flexibility and locks in higher debt service costs during a period when interest rates remain elevated. This limits the council's ability to respond to cost pressures or revenue shortfalls.
findings.figures: £30.8m external borrowing over three years (£12.6m increase from prior three-year period), interest rate assumption 5.3%
findings.quote: Table 3, above, forecasts shows that £30.8m external borrowing  will be required over three years to fund the capital programme. This is an increa se of £12. 6m compared to the equivalent three -year period in 2025/26. This is due to decreased usage of reserves to fund projects.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026/27
findings.headline: Capital programme requires £23.5m additional net financing over three years; being funded from reserves rather than external borrowing
findings.detail: Capital financing requirement grows from £83.2m to £106.7m (Table 1, section 3.1). External borrowing is declining (£53.8m to £51.3m), so the gap is funded by internal borrowing—drawing down treasury investments from £42.6m to £34.9m forecast by 2028/29. Internal borrowing rises from £29.4m to £55.4m.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund capital reduces financial flexibility and buffers. Investment balances shrinking limits future investment income (forecast budget £555,742) and ability to absorb financial shocks. Eventually external borrowing will need to increase substantially to fund the growing CFR and replenish depleted reserves.
findings.figures: Table 1: CFR growing £83.2m→£106.7m; external borrowing £53.8m→£51.3m; internal borrowing £29.4m→£55.4m; treasury investments £42.6m→£34.9m by 2028/29
findings.quote: The Council's current strategy is to maintain borrowing and investments below their underlying levels, sometimes known as internal borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 - Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026/27
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account will require external borrowing from 2026/27 onwards to fund the capital programme
findings.detail: The liability benchmark forecast (section 3.10 and Table 2) shows the HRA moving from a position of no external borrowing requirement to requiring loans from 2026/27 onwards, with net loans requirement reaching £16.4m by 2028/29. This represents a change in position for the HRA.
findings.matters: The HRA is typically self-financing from rental income. Emerging requirement to borrow externally signals either a rising capital programme (new build, major works) or pressure on housing revenue after management costs. A lender would want to understand why this is changing.
findings.figures: Liability benchmark Table 2: HRA net loans requirement forecast at £0m (31.3.26), rising to £16.4m (31.3.29)
findings.quote: The HRA will likely require borrowing from 2026/27 to fund the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 General Fund Budget and Council Tax Council Report
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand continues to rise with limited cost mitigation
findings.detail: The council faces rising demand for homelessness services, including temporary accommodation, with no fully effective cost controls identified. A charging pilot is mentioned as a potential demand-management tool, but this is still experimental. The paper acknowledges 'the continued failure to fully address temporary accommodation subsidy shortfalls'.
findings.matters: Homelessness costs are a leading indicator of financial stress across councils nationally. Rising demand combined with uncertain mitigation signals a service under pressure that could accelerate if economic conditions worsen.
findings.figures: £384k Temporary Accommodation Fund contingency created in 2026/27 budget
findings.quote: National demand for Homelessness services continues to increase and this is replicated, to some extent, locally. Although this is likely to mean greater costs to the Council, the Council continues to explore ways to manage demand, through its preventative work

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 General Fund Budget and Council Tax Council Report
findings.headline: Council's prior audit disclaimers reflect weaknesses that have not yet been fully resolved
findings.detail: The council's external auditors have previously issued disclaimed opinions on historic financial statements. While the council states these did not identify weaknesses in financial sustainability, the fact that accounts have not yet been signed off remains a governance issue. The Statement of Accounts 2024/25 was only published in January 2026, behind the statutory deadline.
findings.matters: Audit disclaimers and delayed accounts completion indicate historical control or reporting weaknesses. For a lender, unaudited or disclaimed accounts create uncertainty about the reliability of the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Accounts published August 2025 (2023/24) and January 2026 (2024/25); statutory backstop dates originally earlier
findings.quote: The Council's external auditors have previously issued disclaimed opinions on historic financial statements. The Statement of Accounts 2023/24 and 2024/25 were published in August 2025 and January 2026 respectively ensuring compliance with the backstop dates.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 General Fund Budget and Council Tax Council Report
findings.headline: Whitwick special expenses area facing a deficit from declining burial fee income
findings.detail: The Whitwick special expenses account has fallen into deficit due to reduced burial fee income from previous years. The council plans to recover this through precept increases over two years, but this represents a service income that has failed to meet expectations.
findings.matters: Declining income from a previously reliable source (burial fees) raises questions about assumptions elsewhere in the budget, particularly around 'at risk' external income streams.
findings.figures: Precept increase of £4.21 (50% increase) from £8.41 to £12.62 Band D for Whitwick
findings.quote: For Whitwick, the deficit has arisen due to a reduction in previous years burial fee income. The proposal is to increase the precept over the next two years along with a review of the Planned and Preventative Maintenance (PPM) to enable the recovery of the deficit.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 General Fund Budget and Council Tax Council Report
findings.headline: Local Plan examination carries cost overrun risk with substantial exposure if the plan is found unsound
findings.detail: The council has already exceeded initial budget estimates for Local Plan examination costs (£85k budgeted). The plan must be submitted by December 2026. The paper explicitly flags that 'if the Local Plan is found unsound at Examination, or if it is not possible to submit by December 2026, the Council will need to decide whether to prepare a Local Plan under the Government's new plan-making system. The costs of this are uncertain but can be expected to be substantial.'
findings.matters: A strategic planning risk with undefined but 'substantial' financial consequences. Failure to deliver the plan on time creates an unquantified future liability and could delay economic development and capital receipts.
findings.figures: £85k Local Plan Examination costs budgeted; additional unforeseen costs already incurred
findings.quote: Costs associated with the statutory examination of the Local Plan, including inspector fees and legal support, have exceeded initial estimates. If the Local Plan is found 'unsound' at Examination, or if it is not possible to submit by December 2026, the Council will need to decide whether to prepare a Local Plan under the Government's new plan-making system. The costs of this are uncertain but can be expected to be substantial.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 General Fund Budget and Council Tax Council Report
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility grant (£2.1m) is expected to decline annually
findings.detail: The council budgets for £2.1m from the EPR grant for waste services in 2026/27. findings.matters: A £2.1m income stream that is contractually declining creates planning uncertainty and potential future budget gaps. This is the type of diminishing income stream that can create sudden pressures if not planned for.
findings.figures: £2.1m EPR grant 2026/27; declining annually

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 General Fund Budget and Council Tax Council Report
findings.headline: Refuse collection service facing significant operational cost pressures from sickness and fleet age
findings.detail: The waste service is experiencing multiple cost pressures totalling over £467k in 2026/27: agency staffing (£170k) and overtime/casual cover (£147k) due to higher-than-anticipated sickness levels, plus vehicle hire costs (£150k) because the existing fleet is ageing with increased mechanical failures. These represent unavoidable cost increases beyond original budget.
findings.matters: A statutory service facing escalating operational costs due to workforce sickness and aging assets suggests either inadequate contingency planning or emerging service sustainability issues. A lender would be concerned whether similar pressures exist elsewhere.

findings.quote: Refuse and Recycling – Increased Agency Costs Due to Sickness – £170k. Higher-than-anticipated sickness levels within the waste collection workforce have necessitated the use of agency staff to maintain service continuity. findings.paper_title: 2026/27 General Fund Budget and Council Tax Council Report
findings.headline: Marlborough Centre capital project cost has overrun by £1.84m
findings.detail: The Marlborough Centre purchase and refurbishment project, commenced in 2021, has seen a significant cost increase identified through detailed surveys and contractor engagement. The additional costs are driven by additional works discovered post-purchase, tenant compensation payments during conversion, and construction cost inflation between 2021 and 2026.
findings.matters: A capital project overrun of this scale indicates either weak initial estimation or emerging construction/regulatory issues. For a lender, this demonstrates project delivery risk and potential cash flow pressures on a regeneration scheme.
findings.figures: £1.84m additional cost above original estimate
findings.quote: the likely cost to complete the project will be approximately £1.84m million higher than originally anticipated. The key reasons for this increase are: Additional works identified following detailed inspections and surveys undertaken post-purchase. Compensation payments required for tenants unable to trade during periods of conversion and refurbishment. Construction cost inflation between 2021 and 2026.

findings.paper_title: 2026/27 General Fund Budget and Council Tax Council Report
findings.headline: Business rates reset benefit is time-limited; a substantial funding gap looms after 2028/29
findings.detail: The council has benefited from strong business rates growth under the new reset arrangements, generating a £14m surplus for 2026/27. However, the council explicitly warns that 'the transitional arrangements currently in place are scheduled to end after the 2028/29 financial year' and cautions against investing heavily in recurring expenditure. The paper notes a projected shortfall of around £2m for 2028/29 (down from over £4m initially), meaning this relief does not solve the underlying structural challenge.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council faces a material structural deficit after the temporary funding arrangements expire, which could limit borrowing capacity and require future service reductions.
findings.figures: £14m surplus 2026/27; £2m projected shortfall 2028/29; transitional support ends 2028/29
findings.quote: the transitional arrangements currently in place are scheduled to end after the 2028/29 financial year. As such, it is prudent for the Council to ensure that a balanced budget is maintained beyond this period. Investing heavily in ongoing or recurring expenditure at this stage would not be appropriate, as it risks creating an unbalanced budget once the transitional support is withdrawn

findings.detail: North West Leicestershire underwent its first Regulator of Social Housing inspection in August 2025, receiving a C2 consumer grade (published November 2025). This indicates material compliance issues with the new regulatory standards. An improvement plan is in place with oversight from Housing Improvement Board, with April 2026 delivery target, but the grade reflects current service deficiencies.
